title: Tane Separates Sky and Earth
text:
In the Maori account, Rangi the Sky Father and Papa the Earth Mother once lay locked together in a close embrace. Their many children were born and lived between them, crowded in a cramped darkness where no light could reach.

The children grew tired of the darkness and began to discuss what to do. Tumatauenga, the fierce one, wanted to kill their parents. Tane Mahuta, father of the forests and birds, said it was better to separate them: let the sky stand far above, and let the earth remain close below as their nursing mother. All the brothers agreed except Tawhirimatea, father of the winds and storms.

One by one the brothers tried to push their parents apart. Rongo tried, then Tangaroa, then Haumia, then Tu. None could. Last came Tane. He placed his head against his mother Earth and his feet against his father Sky, and slowly, steadily, he pushed. Rangi and Papa cried out in grief at being torn apart. But Tane did not stop until the Sky was lifted high above.

Light flooded in for the first time, and the world could grow. Still the parents grieve: Rangi's tears fall as rain and dew, and Papa's sighs rise up as mist. And Tawhirimatea, angry at what his brothers had done, followed his father into the sky and still makes war on them with storms.
lesson: Children need room to grow, even when making it hurts the parents who hold them close. Separation can be an act of love on both sides.
people: Rangi (Ranginui), Papa (Papatuanuku), Tane Mahuta, Tawhirimatea, Tumatauenga
source: George Grey, Polynesian Mythology (1855), The Children of Heaven and Earth
